meta.title: TENKA: Physics-Guided Multimodal Deep Learning for Bolide Detection from Geostationary Satellite Observations

abstract: Bolide detection from geostationary satellite observations is a challenging problem due to the overwhelming prevalence of lightning and meteorological optical emissions. Existing approaches rely primarily on rule-based filtering or physics-driven machine learning, often trading detection sensitivity for precision. We present TENKA a physics-guided multimodal deep learning architecture that integrates spatial–spectral ABI imagery, temporal GLM event sequences, and physics-inspired summary features derived from GLM group evolution. TENKA jointly exploits morphological cues, temporal coherence, and physically meaningful constraints associated with meteoroid atmospheric entry. Evaluated on a curated dataset of 2,000 manually vetted bolides and 2,000 non-bolide flashes, the approach achieves an AUC of 0.9983 and a recall of 0.983. Under a simulated real-world imbalance representative of operational GLM observations, TENKA model significantly reduces false positives compared to purely data-driven DL baselines while maintaining high sensitivity. These results highlight the importance of integrating domain-informed physical descriptors within deep learning frameworks for robust aerospace event detection.

blocks.html: Bolides are exceptionally bright meteors produced by meteoroids entering Earth’s atmosphere. They provide important information on impact hazards for planetary defense and act as natural probes of atmospheric physics. Continuous observations from geostationary satellites such as GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite) from NASA enable large-scale monitoring of transient optical events, offering an opportunity to automatically identify bolides alongside lightning and meteorological phenomena. However, automated detection remains challenging due to the extreme rarity of bolides compared to lightning flashes and the visual similarity between these events from satellite observations.

Early operational pipelines have relied on heuristic filters or physics-driven algorithms applied to geostationary lightning mapper (GLM) data [1]. While these approaches achieve high precision, they often miss a substantial fraction of true events when configured with conservative thresholds intended to minimize false positives. More recent physics-based machine learning (ML) methods [2] improve sensitivity but remain limited by handcrafted features and the absence of context from multispectral imagery. At the same time, deep learning (DL) models combining convolutional and recurrent architectures have shown strong performance in lightning forecasting [3, 4], yet dedicated solutions for bolide detection remain largely unexplored.

Bolides exhibit distinctive physical properties, (including ballistic motion, coherent temporal evolution, and gradual energy deposition) during atmospheric ablation. Motivated by this observation, we propose TENKA, a physics-guided multimodal neural network (NN) that integrates advanced baseline imager (ABI) imagery, GLM temporal sequences, and physics-inspired summary features within a unified framework.
The main contributions of this work are threefold:
• A multimodal DL architecture that jointly models spatial, temporal, and physics-based information for bolide detection.
• The integration of trajectory- and energy-consistency features derived from GLM group evolution into a neural framework.
• A realistic evaluation under simulated operational class imbalance demonstrating improved false positive suppression while maintaining high recall.

Early efforts to detect bolides from geostationary satellite data have primarily relied on physics-driven filtering and classical ML. Rumpf et al. [1, 5] introduced a rule-based algorithm exploiting trajectory consistency and energy characteristics in GLM observations, demonstrating the feasibility of automated bolide discovery. While effective when carefully tuned, threshold-based pipelines require manual parameter adjustment and can be less flexible than data-driven learning approaches when adapting to different datasets or operational conditions. Building on this work, Smith et al. [2] proposed an automated pipeline incorporating physics-inspired features and a random forest classifier, improving detection capability while retaining interpretability.

Beyond detection, subsequent studies have analyzed systematic biases inherent to GLM observations when applied to bolide populations. Ozerov et al. [5] developed a Bayesian framework to quantify instrumental biases and estimate latitudinal variations in bolide flux, highlighting the importance of accounting for sensor-dependent effects in statistical analyses. More recently, Kokou [6] demonstrated that bolide signatures can be extracted from the Meteosat Third Generation Lightning Imager, further underscoring the growing relevance of space-based optical lightning sensors for meteor science.

In parallel, DL approaches have achieved significant success in lightning detection and convective storm analysis using multispectral geostationary satellite imagery [4, 7]. Recurrent-convolutional architectures have further been used to model the temporal evolution of convective systems and forecast lightning occurrence [3], while attention-based multimodal networks have shown improved performance in local lightning prediction tasks [8]. These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of multimodal DL for atmospheric transients but focus primarily on meteorological phenomena.

Despite these advances, DL approaches tailored specifically to bolide detection from geostationary satellite observations remain largely unexplored. Existing pipelines rely primarily on handcrafted rules or shallow models, while DL studies in related domains focus mainly on lightning forecasting and do not incorporate the ballistic motion or energy deposition patterns characteristic of meteoroid entry. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has combined multimodal satellite inputs with physics-guided constraints within a unified neural architecture. The present work addresses this gap by introducing TENKA, a physics-guided multimodal network that jointly models spatial morphology, temporal evolution, and trajectory-consistent physical descriptors.

TENKA is a physics-guided multimodal NN for bolide detection that integrates three complementary information sources: ABI multispectral imagery, GLM temporal event sequences, and physics-inspired descriptors derived from GLM group evolution (Fig. 1).
As no public benchmark exists for bolide detection from geostationary data, we constructed a dataset from GOES observations using GLM and ABI measurements.

We selected 2,000 confirmed bolides from the NASA human-vetted database [9] and extracted the corresponding GLM event sequences based on reported time and location. For each event, a six-channel ABI infrared patch, with bands 8–10 (water vapor, ∼6.2–7.3 µm) and 13–15 (infrared window, ∼10.3–12.3 µm), was retrieved at the flash position from the most recent acquisition preceding the event.

Negative samples (2,000) were generated by randomly sampling locations and times within the GOES-16-17-18-19 coverage. For each case, the nearest GLM flash in space and time was selected, and its location was used to extract the corresponding ABI patch, ensuring realistic lightning-like negatives.

The final dataset comprises 4,000 samples and was split into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% test sets. Model selection was performed on the validation split, with the test set reserved for final evaluation.

ABI observations are provided as fixed-size image patches composed of six infrared channels. A ResNet backbone (ResNet-34) is employed as a convolutional feature extractor. The first convolutional layer is modified to accept the six ABI channels in input. The final classification layer is removed, and the globally pooled feature vector is projected through a fully connected head consisting of a linear layer, batch normalization, ReLU activation, and dropout. This produces a compact embedding zABI encoding spatial– multispectral thermal structure.
GLM data are represented as variable-length sequences of event-level features describing spatial position, timing, and emitted energy.

A multi-layer bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) processes packed sequences to efficiently handle varying sequence lengths. The final GLM embedding zGLM is obtained by concatenating the last hidden states of the forward and backward directions, allowing the network to capture both early-to-late and late-to-early temporal context.

In addition to learned representations, the model incorporates an explicit physics modality derived from GLM group evolution statistics. Inspired by prior rule-based and physics-driven approaches [2], an 8-dimensional feature vector xphys summarizes trajectory coherence, temporal structure, and energy deposition behavior:
• Number of GLM groups and event duration (scale and persistence),
• Linear trajectory fit residual and normalized deviation from linear motion (ballistic consistency),
• Energy balance time and polynomial energy–time fit residual (ablation dynamics),
• Logarithm of total emitted energy and energy smoothness (temporal coherence).

These descriptors encode trajectory consistency and energy evolution patterns typical of meteoroid entry, complementing learned representations. The physics vector is projected into a compact embedding zphys using a lightweight two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) with ReLU activation and dropout regularization.

Late fusion is intentionally adopted to preserve modality-specific structure and prevent visually dominant modalities from overwhelming physically informative but lowdimensional descriptors. This design choice improves robustness under extreme class imbalance, where rare highenergy lightning events may otherwise produce false positives.

The fused representation is passed through a lightweight MLP classifier composed of two fully connected layers with ReLU activation and dropout regularization, producing a single logit corresponding to the probability to produce the final bolide likelihood.

The model was trained using cross-entropy loss for binary classification. Hyperparameters, including the ResNet backbone, GRU hidden size, embedding dimensionality, and regularization parameters, were selected based on validation set performance. All inputs were normalized using statistics computed from the training set.

Table 1 compares TENKA against ablated variants and previously proposed approaches from the literature. Baselines include a GRU model operating only on GLM temporal data, a multimodal DL model without physics features, a physics-based random forest classifier inspired by Smith et al. [2], and the rule-based filtering strategy proposed by Rumpf et al. [1].

TENKA achieves the highest area under the curve (AUC) and F1 score among all evaluated approaches, demonstrating that physics-guided multimodal fusion yields the strongest overall performance. Notably, the multimodal architecture without physics features exhibits a higher false positive rate despite strong balanced-set performance, highlighting the importance of explicitly encoding physical constraints.

Comparing TENKA with the CNN+GRU baseline reveals a substantial reduction in false positives (6 vs. 19) at a comparable recall value. This suggests that the physics-inspired descriptors regularize predictions toward physically consistent trajectories. Similarly, the physics-based random forest approach [2] achieves strong precision but lower recall, indicating that learned multimodal representations improve sensitivity while retaining physical consistency.

blocks.caption: Overview of the proposed TENKA physics-guided multimodal architecture. GLM event sequences are processed by a bidirectional GRU encoder (top branch), ABI multispectral image patches are encoded using a ResNet-34 convolutional NN (middle branch), and physics-inspired features derived from GLM group evolution processed with a MLP (bottom branch). The three modality-specific embeddings are fused through late concatenation and passed to a final MLP for bolide classification.

blocks.html: Ablation experiments highlight the complementary, and sometimes competing, roles of the different modalities. The GLM-only GRU model achieves strong recall with relatively few false positives, indicating that temporal dynamics alone provide a robust baseline for bolide discrimination. Introducing ABI imagery through a purely data-driven multimodal model increases the false positive rate, suggesting that multispectral visual context can introduce ambiguity when not constrained by physical priors. The addition of physics-guided features mitigates this effect, substantially reducing spurious detections and yielding the best overall performance, which indicates that physically informed descriptors help regularize multimodal representations.

Because bolide detection occurs under an extreme classimbalance scenario, balanced evaluation metrics alone are insufficient to assess operational performance. We therefore simulate a realistic deployment scenario by approximating a bolide-to-flash ratio representative of GLM observations.

Under this regime, absolute F1 scores decrease across all learning-based methods, which is expected when false positives dominate the metric computation in extreme rareevent scenarios. However, TENKA maintains the highest real-world F1 and precision among learning-based approaches while preserving a high recall. The rule-based filter [1] achieves high real-world precision and F1 under conservative threshold settings largely because it classifies only the most unambiguous events, resulting in a very low recall. While effective for identifying obvious candidates, such threshold-based pipelines rely on manually tuned parameters that are difficult to generalize across different datasets and operational conditions. In practice, adapting these approaches requires substantial manual adjustment and domain expertise, making it challenging to maintain a consistent detection performance at scale.

These results indicate that integrating physics-informed descriptors into a multimodal DL framework not only improves the balance between sensitivity and false positive suppression, but also achieves the strongest overall performance among learning-based approaches, highlighting its suitability for practical aerospace applications.

TENKA achieves strong detection performance while maintaining robustness against false positives, a key requirement for operational bolide monitoring. By learning adaptive decision boundaries while incorporating physically meaningful constraints, the model reduces reliance on manual threshold tuning and enables scalable deployment within existing geostationary processing pipelines. Because the architecture relies only on sensor modalities already available on current platforms, it is directly applicable to future missions such as Meteosat Third Generation (MTG). Future work will explore cross-sensor generalization and uncertainty-aware predictions to further support operational deployment.

We presented TENKA, a physics-guided multimodal framework for bolide detection from geostationary satellite observations that integrates ABI imagery, GLM temporal dynamics, and physics-inspired descriptors within a unified neural architecture. By combining learned representations with physically grounded constraints, the proposed approach achieves strong detection performance while improving robustness under extreme class imbalance and reducing false positives relative to purely data-driven multimodal models.

TENKA remains compatible with current geostationary processing pipelines and provides a scalable path toward automated monitoring of atmospheric entry events. Future work will focus on cross-sensor generalization and the extension of the framework to the MTG mission, enabling bolide detection capabilities over Europe and Africa and supporting next-generation operational space situational awareness.
